title: Annotatio I §.III: Scultetus grants tropum in the Cup words but denies consequence for the rest — Strimesius replies
pass_a_gloss: Nor will any Lutheran deny it — certainly not Dom. Daniel Severinus Scultetus in the still recent Discussion of Reformed Universalism, meanwhile denying the consequence: I will grant, he says, that in these words (namely of the second or posterior part of the Institution of the Sacred Supper) there is a trope; the remaining things pertaining to the Institution of the Sacred Eucharist are not for that reason to be taken tropically. For the proper sense of words is everywhere to be retained unless a grave cause obstructs, which here — namely in the proposition of the prior Part This is my body — there is none. With which words, as the most distinguished man will have agreed with me that the Eucharistic proposition This cup is the N.T. in my blood consists of not one trope, so much the more will he have agreed, not having merely posited it, the more he will have annotated from Heb. 9:17 & 20 that this mode of speaking emulates Moses’ formula when he purified the whole people and sprinkled them with blood, sounding thus: This is the blood of the N.T. enjoined by God;
pass_b_english: Scultetus, in his recent Discussion of Reformed Universalism, grants a trope in those second-part Institution words, yet denies the consequence for the rest of the Eucharist Institution.
Proper sense, he says, is kept everywhere unless a grave cause blocks it — and in This is my body, he claims, there is none.
Strimesius notes he already agrees the Cup proposition is built of more than one trope, and all the more once Heb. 9:17, 20 shows it emulates Moses’ This is the blood of the N.T.
source_text: Nec abnuet Lutheranus quivis, certè non Dominus Daniel Severinus Scultetus in Discussione Universalismi Reformati adhuc recenti, consequentiam interim abnuens: Ponam inquit, in his verbis (partis scil. Institutionis sacrae Coenae, secundae, seu posterioris) esse tropum, non sunt eam ob causam reliqua ad Sacrae Eucharistiae institutionem pertinentia tropicè accipienda. Proprius enim verborum sensus ubivis est retinendus, ni gravis obstet causa, quae hic, scilicet in propositione prioris Partis: Hoc est corpus meum, nulla est. Quibus verbis, uti mihi consenserit Clariss. vir, propositionem Eucharisticam: Hoc poculum est N. T. in sanguine meo, tropô non uno constare, tantôque magis consenserit, non nude posuerit, quantô ex Hebr. cap. 9. vers. 17. & 20. magis annotaverit, modum hunc loquendi aemulari formulam dicendi Mosis, cùm populum totum expiaret, & sanguine aspergeret, ita sonantem: Hic est sanguis N. T. à Deo injuncti;

rejected: denying the sequence of events only

notes: Scultetus grants Cup tropum; denies rest; Heb 9.
